speaker: maya
text: Last time: what crossed the Atlantic in both directions, and the cargo nobody chose. This time: England starts planting, not just raiding. Jamestown, 1607. A company town that starved, nearly quit, and survived. Four boxes: Jamestown, tobacco, the House of Burgesses, and 1619, the year the assembly and the slave ship arrived together. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Twelve minutes, and you'll check all four off.

speaker: marcus
text: Start with the money, because no king paid for Jamestown. London merchants formed a joint-stock company, the Virginia Company: a pool of private money chasing a profit. James the First signed the charter in 1606 — the crown's permission, in writing. But the cash was theirs, and so was the risk.

speaker: maya
text: Wait, I always assumed the crown just sent them. The king's colony, the king's money.

speaker: marcus
text: The king's charter, the merchants' money. Nobody's money but theirs was on the line — which is exactly why the payoff could be enormous. Private money, private risk. That was the whole deal.

speaker: maya
text: So who actually got on the boats?

speaker: marcus
text: About a hundred and five men and boys, on three ships. They landed in the spring of 1607 on a swampy peninsula up the James River. And the site was a trade-off: easy to defend, with deep water right at the shore, and terrible for everything else. Marsh, mosquitoes, and brackish river water.

speaker: maya
text: I got sick off lake water on one camping trip in fifth grade, and I still won't drink from a thermos that smells funny. These people had no choice.

speaker: marcus
text: They paid for it. Bad water, fever, dysentery. Within months, more than half of them were dead. And here's the part that stings: most were gentlemen. Sons of gentry, jewelers, men who'd never held a plow. They came hunting gold, not planting wheat. One of them wrote that in camp there was nothing but …dig gold, refine gold, load gold.

speaker: maya
text: Digging for gold. In Virginia.

speaker: marcus
text: Iron pyrite, mostly. Fool's gold. Which is where John Smith comes in. He takes over in the fall of 1608 and lays down the law: "He that will not work, shall not eat." Plant, build, or starve.

speaker: maya
text: Cold.

speaker: marcus
text: It worked. Then, in the fall of 1609, Smith's gunpowder bag catches fire. He's badly burned, and he sails home to England. The colony falls apart without him.

speaker: maya
text: What about the famous rescue? Pocahontas saving Smith's life?

speaker: marcus
text: Smith told that story years later: captured by the Powhatan and about to be executed, when the chief's daughter steps in. Some scholars think he made it up. Others think it was a ceremony he misunderstood, an adoption, not an execution. Nobody's fully sure.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. A camp full of gentlemen who came hunting gold, nobody planting anything, and the one man enforcing work just sailed home. It's the winter of 1609. What happens next?

speaker: maya
text: They starve. About five hundred settlers go into that winter. About sixty come out. They ate dogs, horses, shoe leather. The archaeology says some ate each other.

speaker: marcus
text: The starving time. And in the spring of 1610, the survivors actually quit. They boarded ships for England, and on the way out they ran into the new governor, De La Warr, sailing in with three ships, about a hundred and fifty fresh colonists, and supplies. He turned them around.

speaker: maya
text: Imagine quitting and running into your replacement on the way out the door. Wait — Delaware. That's him, right? The state?

speaker: marcus
text: The bay, the river, and the state. All named for him.

speaker: maya
text: So the exam question writes itself. Why did Jamestown almost die: the swamp, or the people?

speaker: marcus
text: The people. The swamp hurt, but the gold-fever killed. If a question asks for the cause, pick the gentlemen who wouldn't plant over the geography.

speaker: maya
text: And the common mistake for box one: don't write that the king funded Jamestown. London merchants did, on a royal charter.

speaker: marcus
text: So how does this place not just die forever? One plant. John Rolfe, the same man who'd later marry Pocahontas, starts growing tobacco around 1612. Not the harsh native leaf. A sweeter Caribbean strain, from seeds out of Trinidad.

speaker: maya
text: Rolfe the tobacco guy is Rolfe the husband guy.

speaker: marcus
text: Same guy. And it worked: within a few years, Virginia tobacco was selling in London, and the colony finally had a reason to exist. The answer was a weed.

speaker: maya
text: Didn't the king hate smoking, though?

speaker: marcus
text: James wrote a whole pamphlet against it in 1604, A Counterblaste to Tobacco. Called it a vile custom. James's pamphlet never stood a chance against the money.

speaker: maya
text: So the Disney version: how much of it survives?

speaker: marcus
text: Almost none of it. The English captured Pocahontas in 1613. She married Rolfe in 1614, and that bought a few years of peace. She died in England in 1617, about twenty years old.

speaker: maya
text: Okay, but a plant doesn't plant itself. Who's working these fields?

speaker: marcus
text: Tobacco needed land and workers, and workers needed paying. The company's answer, in 1618, was the headright: fifty acres to anyone who paid a settler's passage. Bring ten workers, claim five hundred acres.

speaker: maya
text: So the workers each got fifty acres for coming over?

speaker: marcus
text: The person who paid got the acres. The boss, not the boat ride. The engine ran like this: planters import workers, workers become acres, acres grow tobacco.

speaker: maya
text: And the workers signed up for this?

speaker: marcus
text: They signed away four to seven years of labor for the passage over: indentured servants, most of them young, poor, and English. The majority of English migrants to the Chesapeake came this way.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. Tobacco exhausts the soil fast. Every few years, a planter needs fresh fields. Fresh fields have to come from somewhere. Where?

speaker: maya
text: Powhatan land. The colony keeps planting past every boundary it agreed to. Remember that. It's loaded for later.

speaker: marcus
text: One exam warning for box two: when a question pairs tobacco with a labor system, connect them instead of memorizing two facts. The headright buys the passage; the indenture pays it off.

speaker: maya
text: And the common mistake: the headright gave land to the planter who paid, not the servant who sailed. Two boxes down.

speaker: marcus
text: Now, who's running this place? For the first decade, the company, from London. Then, in the summer of 1619, the company lets the colony elect an assembly: the House of Burgesses. Burgess just means representative.

speaker: maya
text: The company just handed over power?

speaker: marcus
text: It traded a little power for a lot of settlers. An elected assembly made Virginia look stable and permanent. That permanence is what turned cautious investors into steady profits back in London.

speaker: maya
text: So 1619 is the democracy year.

speaker: marcus
text: Careful. At first, all free adult men could vote, but the franchise narrowed over time, and it never included women, servants, or anyone enslaved. It's self-government, not democracy as we'd mean it.

speaker: maya
text: Common mistake for box three, then: don't write that everyone voted. Free men voted, and even that narrowed.

speaker: marcus
text: And the exam point: if a question asks what the Burgesses prove, the answer is that English colonists expected a say in their government, even under a company charter, an ocean from the king.

speaker: maya
text: Same year, though — 1619. Wait, wasn't something else arriving that year too?

speaker: marcus
text: Late that August, a privateer ship called the White Lion pulled into Point Comfort. A privateer is a pirate with a government's permission slip. This one sailed under Dutch papers and carried about twenty Africans, seized from a Portuguese slave ship. Rolfe wrote it down himself: "20 and odd" Africans, traded for food.

speaker: maya
text: So that's the start of slavery in Virginia?

speaker: marcus
text: The start of Africans in Virginia, and the status is murky. On paper they were sold as servants. In reality they'd been stolen twice over, and nobody asked them. But most field workers for decades after were still indentured servants, not enslaved Africans. The full racial slave system comes later in the century.

speaker: maya
text: Same year. An assembly votes, and a slave ship lands.

speaker: marcus
text: The contradiction at the start of English America. And it gets bloodier. Tobacco keeps eating land, the English keep planting past the boundary lines, and in March of 1622, Opechancanough, Powhatan's successor, coordinates a surprise attack across the plantations. Three hundred and forty-seven dead. About a quarter of the colony, in a single day.

speaker: maya
text: A quarter. The Powhatan just snapped?

speaker: marcus
text: They'd watched the English plant past every boundary for fifteen years. "Snapped" makes it sound sudden. It wasn't.

speaker: marcus
text: The English answered with years of war: poisoned wine at a parley the next year, burned villages. And back in London, the king had seen enough. In 1624, James revoked the company's charter and made Virginia a royal colony. But Jamestown survived, because by then tobacco paid for everything.

speaker: maya
text: One more exam warning, box four: the 1619 double event is built for a compare question. An assembly voting while a slave ship unloads — same year. If they ask what it shows, the answer is the contradiction starting early.

speaker: maya
text: And the common mistake: 1619 didn't make Virginia a slave colony overnight. Servants still worked most of the fields for decades.

speaker: maya
text: All four are on the board. Four boxes, let's land them. One: Jamestown. Sixteen-oh-seven, company money, swamp site, gold-fever gentlemen. Smith's rule held it together until 1609, the starving time nearly finished it, and De La Warr turned the quitters around in 1610.

speaker: maya
text: Box one, checked. Two: tobacco. Rolfe's Caribbean strain, around 1612. The headright hands fifty acres a head to whoever pays the passage, the planter who paid, not the servant who sailed, and indentured servants work the fields for four to seven years.

speaker: maya
text: Box two, checked. Three: the House of Burgesses, summer 1619. First elected assembly in English America. Free men voted at first. Not everyone, and it narrowed.

speaker: maya
text: Box three, checked. Four: 1619. The White Lion lands "20 and odd" Africans at Point Comfort. And that's when the slave system starts?

speaker: marcus
text: The first Africans arrive that year. The system comes decades later.

speaker: maya
text: Right. Arrivals in 1619, system decades later. And three years after that, 1622: Opechancanough's attack kills about a quarter of the colony, and the company loses its charter in 1624.

speaker: maya
text: Box four, checked.

speaker: maya
text: Three questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it.

speaker: maya
text: One. A colonist wrote that in the Jamestown camp there was nothing but …dig gold, refine gold, load gold. What's the point of this source: why did Jamestown nearly starve?

speaker: maya
text: The settlers chased gold instead of planting food — gentlemen hunting iron pyrite while the food stores ran out. The cause was human, not geographic: gold-fever beat the swamp.

speaker: maya
text: Two. A planter pays the passage for six servants and claims three hundred acres. Name the system, and say who benefits.

speaker: maya
text: The headright system — fifty acres a head, six heads, three hundred acres. The giveaway is who benefits: the planter who paid. The servants get years of labor, not land.

speaker: maya
text: Three. 1619: an assembly meets in Jamestown, and the White Lion lands "20 and odd" Africans at Point Comfort. A historian pairs these two events. What's the argument?

speaker: maya
text: Self-government and forced labor arrived together — the House of Burgesses and the White Lion, same year. The contradiction at the start of English America: the vote and the slave ship, side by side.

speaker: maya
text: One more, fast. Virginia becomes a royal colony in 1624. Whose charter got revoked?

speaker: maya
text: The Virginia Company's. The king took it back after the wars and the death toll.

speaker: maya
text: One thing to carry forward: they came hunting gold, and a weed saved them. Then it demanded land and workers until it broke the peace. Check your four boxes. Next time: rewind sixty years, to the silver mountain that bankrolled the Spanish Empire.

speaker: marcus
text: They sailed here hunting gold —

speaker: maya
text: and ended up planting themselves.
